title: Fundamentals of computer networks flash cards

cards.front: Define a computer network.
back: Two or more computers or devices connected so they can communicate and share resources.

cards.front: Which network type uses Bluetooth in this specification?
back: Personal Area Network (PAN).

cards.front: Which protocol is used to send email?
back: SMTP.

cards.front: Which protocol addresses and routes packets?
back: IP.

cards.front: At which TCP/IP layer does TCP operate?
back: Transport layer.

cards.front: Which cable type carries data as light?
back: Fibre-optic cable.

cards.front: Give two advantages of networking computers in a school.
back: Any two of sharing files/printers, central accounts, communication, central backups, shared internet access or central software management.

cards.front: Explain the difference between a LAN and a WAN.
back: A LAN covers a relatively small area and is usually managed by one organisation.
A WAN covers a wide area and often uses infrastructure under distributed ownership.

cards.front: Explain the difference between HTTP and HTTPS.
back: Both transfer web data.
HTTPS encrypts the connection and supports authentication, making data in transit more secure.

cards.front: Explain the difference between SMTP and IMAP.
back: SMTP sends email to a mail server or between servers.
IMAP accesses and manages email stored on a server.

cards.front: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of a wireless network.
back: It supports mobility and avoids a cable to each device.
It may suffer interference, reduced range/performance or greater interception risk.

cards.front: Explain why authentication and encryption are both useful.
back: Authentication checks the identity of someone requesting access.
Encryption makes intercepted data unreadable without the required key.

cards.front: Explain why fibre-optic cable may be chosen for a long, high-traffic network link.
back: Fibre supports high bandwidth.
It can carry signals over long distances.
It is not affected by electromagnetic interference in the way copper can be.

cards.front: Describe what a firewall does.
back: It monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic.
It compares traffic with defined security rules.
It allows or blocks traffic according to those rules.

cards.front: Explain how MAC address filtering controls network access and give one limitation.
back: Filtering compares an adapter’s MAC address with allow or block rules. It controls devices rather than identifying their current users. An address can be copied or spoofed, so use it with authentication and encryption.

cards.front: State the job of the application, transport and internet layers.
back: Application: provides services used by network applications.
Transport: sets up end-to-end communication and manages packet delivery.
Internet: addresses and routes packets across networks.

cards.front: Explain why protocols are needed.
back: Protocols provide agreed communication rules so different devices can interpret exchanged data. The rules can cover formatting, addressing, transmission and responses to errors; each protocol handles its particular part of the job.

cards.front: Give three disadvantages of computer networks.
back: Any three of setup/maintenance cost, dependence on shared services, security risk, malware spread, congestion, privacy concerns or need for skilled administration.

cards.front: Compare wired and wireless connections for classroom computers.
back: Wired links are normally stable, low latency and less affected by radio interference.
They restrict device location and require cable installation.
Wireless links support mobile devices and are easier to extend.
Wireless performance can fall because of distance, obstacles, interference and congestion, and strong security is required.

cards.front: Describe how the four TCP/IP layers take part when a browser requests a web page.
back: The application layer creates an HTTP or HTTPS request.
TCP at the transport layer manages the end-to-end communication.
IP at the internet layer adds addressing and routes packets.
The link layer transmits data using the local NIC and network hardware.

cards.front: Explain how several network-security methods work together.
back: Authentication limits access to recognised users.
Encryption protects data if traffic is intercepted.
A firewall blocks traffic that breaks defined rules.
MAC filtering can restrict devices, so the combined controls cover identity, data, connections and hardware access.

cards.front: A business has offices in two cities. Explain why its internal city-office networks are LANs while the connection between cities forms part of a WAN.
back: Each office LAN covers a relatively small local area.
Each LAN can be owned and managed by the business.
The inter-city connection spans a wide geographical area.
It is likely to use telecommunications infrastructure owned or managed by other organisations.

cards.front: Expand TCP and name its TCP/IP layer.
back: Transmission Control Protocol; the transport layer. It supports reliable end-to-end communication.

cards.front: Expand IP and name its TCP/IP layer.
back: Internet Protocol; the internet layer. It supports addressing and routing packets.

cards.front: Expand HTTP and HTTPS.
back: HTTP means Hypertext Transfer Protocol. HTTPS means Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure and protects web communication using an encrypted connection.

cards.front: Expand SMTP and IMAP.
back: SMTP means Simple Mail Transfer Protocol. IMAP means Internet Message Access Protocol.

cards.front: Why does reading an email on a phone and seeing its read status on a laptop point to IMAP?
back: IMAP manages a server-held mailbox and synchronises message status and folders across clients. SMTP handles sending instead.

cards.front: Packets arrive out of order and one is missing. Which protocol supports detecting the loss and reconstructing the ordered data?
back: TCP. It supports retransmission of missing data and reconstruction in the correct order. IP provides addressing and routing.

cards.front: Do TCP and IP alone make the contents of a message unreadable to an interceptor?
back: No. Reliability and routing are different from encryption. A suitable encrypted connection is needed to protect readable contents.

cards.front: Why can an HTTPS phishing site still be dangerous?
back: Encryption protects the connection to that site, but does not prove that its owner is trustworthy. A fake site can still request and steal information.

cards.front: What is the difference between plaintext and ciphertext?
back: Plaintext is readable original data. Ciphertext is the encrypted form, which requires the appropriate decryption process and key to recover.

cards.front: Does encryption stop someone intercepting network traffic?
back: It aims to stop an interceptor understanding the contents without the appropriate key. Interception itself can still occur.

cards.front: Expand MAC in MAC address filtering.
back: Media Access Control. Filtering compares network-adapter addresses with configured rules to permit or block devices.

cards.front: Why does allowing a device’s MAC address not prove who is using it?
back: The rule identifies an allowed adapter address rather than a person. Someone else may use that device, and addresses can also be spoofed.

cards.front: What can happen if a firewall rule is too permissive or too restrictive?
back: A permissive rule may allow unwanted traffic. An overly restrictive rule may block legitimate work. Rules must suit the intended service.

cards.front: How does a PAN differ from a LAN in a phone-and-earbuds example?
back: The Bluetooth connection forms a short-range network around one person. A LAN connects devices across a local area such as a home or school.

cards.front: Why does a LAN not become a WAN just because it contains many computers?
back: LAN and WAN describe geographical scale and management, rather than a fixed maximum number of devices.

cards.front: Why might fibre suit a long link near equipment producing electromagnetic interference?
back: Fibre carries light and resists electromagnetic interference. It also supports high bandwidth over long distances, though installation may cost more.

cards.front: Why can replacing a local cable fail to improve internet download speed?
back: Another part of the route may be the bottleneck, such as the internet connection or remote server. The local cable is only one part of the journey.

cards.front: Distinguish bandwidth from latency.
back: Bandwidth is the amount of data a connection can carry per second. Latency is communication delay. A high-bandwidth connection can still have noticeable delay.

cards.front: Name the receiving-device TCP/IP layers in the order data passes up to its application.
back: Link, internet, transport, application. The sender processes the layers in the opposite direction.

cards.front: What is the job of the link layer, and which components belong there?
back: It handles the local connection and network hardware. The network interface card and operating-system device drivers operate here.

cards.front: Why can the local network hardware change without redesigning the email protocol?
back: Layers separate responsibilities behind agreed interfaces. The link layer can change while the application still uses its existing email rules.
